newsitem.title: CANADA: IMF says Canada 1997-98 GDP growth to lead G7.
newsitem.headline: IMF says Canada 1997-98 GDP growth to lead G7.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund said on Wednesday that Canada's real economic growth was likely to lead the Group of Seven industrialized nations in 1997 and 1998.
"The strength of fundamentals in Canada bodes well for continuing recovery in 1997-98, with inflation remaining within the target range," the IMF said in its World Economic Outlook.

It raised its projection for real growth in gross domestic product (GDP) for 1997 to 3.5 percent from the 3.2 percent predicted last autumn and from the 1.5 percent recorded in 1996. For 1998 it estimated 3.4 percent growth. Both were higher than growth rates predicted for other G7 nations.

"In Canada, after a disappointing performance in 1995 and early 1996, economic activity picked up in the second half of last year; unemployment has begun to decline, and the economy is poised for solid growth in 1997 and 1998," it said.
"The general fiscal deficit, which reached 7-1/2 percent of GDP in 1992, has been reduced progressively and is expected to disappear next year.

"This has helped restore financial market confidence, which together with subdued inflation has allowed official interest rates to be reduced well below U.S. money market rates without undermining the credibility of the authorities' commitment to price stability or weakening the exchange rate."
The IMF predicted consumer price inflation would hold unchanged from 1996 at 1.7 percent in 1997 and rise to 1.8 percent in 1998.
Unemployment should fall to 9.4 percent this year and 8.8 percent in 1998 from 9.7 percent in 1996, it said.
It projected the current account swinging from a deficit of US$1.0 billion in 1996 to balance in 1997 and a surplus of $1.0 billion in 1998.
